title: Word Search II
description: Brute force to optimized: an independent DFS backtracking search per word versus a single DFS pass guided by a trie merging every word's shared prefixes.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Given an m by n board of characters and a list of words, return all words from the list that can be formed by a path of adjacent cells (horizontally or vertically), where the same cell may not be used more than once in a single word.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","board (a grid of characters), words (a list of strings)"],["Output","Every word from the list that can be traced out on the board"],["Goal","Search efficiently, without a completely independent search for every single word"],["Constraints","board dimensions up to 12 x 12; up to 30000 words, each up to 10 characters"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["Many words to search for at once on the same board","Merge all words into a single trie, so shared prefixes are explored only once"],["A path of adjacent cells, each used at most once","DFS backtracking, marking cells visited and un-marking them on the way back"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

For every word in the list, determine whether it can be spelled out by moving between horizontally or vertically adjacent cells on the board, never reusing a cell within that one word, and collect every word that succeeds.

blocks.title: Analogy: Searching a Grid for Many Words at Once, Sharing the Search Where Possible
blocks.text: Picture a word-search puzzle grid, and a whole dictionary of words to hunt for at once. Instead of scanning the grid separately for every single word, words that share a common beginning (like "eat" and "eating") can be searched together, branching apart only once their spellings diverge.

blocks.caption: Merging every word into one trie lets shared prefixes be explored only once

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: words = ["oath","pea","eat","rain"]
On the given board, "oath" and "eat" can be traced out via adjacent cells, while "pea" and "rain" cannot.
Edge case: no word in the list can be found
The result is simply an empty list.
5. How Should We Think?
Before searching the board independently for every word, notice that many words in a large list often share common prefixes, and that shared structure can be searched only once.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Searching the board separately for each of up to 30000 words means potentially re-walking many of the same board paths over and over, once per word that happens to share a prefix.

Observation 2: Merging every word into a single trie means all words sharing a prefix share the same trie path, so a single DFS from a board cell can check progress against every word simultaneously.

Observation 3: As the DFS walks the board, it also walks down the trie; whenever the trie has no child matching the next board character, that entire path can be abandoned immediately, since no word continues that way.

Observation 4: Whenever a trie node marks the end of some word, that word has been found on the board and can be recorded.
This leads to building one trie from all the words, then running a single DFS backtracking search from every board cell that simultaneously checks against every word via the shared trie.
6. Brute Force Solution
For each word independently, run a full DFS backtracking search from every board cell, checking if that specific word can be traced out.
Step by step algorithm

items: For every word in the list, try starting the search from every cell on the board.
From a starting cell, recursively check whether the word's next character matches an adjacent unused cell, backtracking whenever a path fails.
If any starting cell succeeds, add the word to the result.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: a completely separate DFS search for every single word

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: exists(word) is a completely self-contained DFS search, with no awareness of any other word being searched for.
Words sharing a long common prefix each re-walk that same prefix on the board independently.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(words.length times rows times cols times 4 to the power word length), a completely fresh DFS search per word.
Space: O(word length) per search, for the recursion stack.
Limitation: with up to 30000 words, many sharing prefixes, this is far too slow; searching board paths for one word's prefix gives no benefit to any other word that shares it.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why searching per word independently is wasteful: words with a shared prefix (like "eat" and "eating") would each re-walk the exact same board path for that shared portion.

What structure merges shared prefixes: a trie built from all the words at once, where common prefixes collapse into the same path through the trie.

How the DFS uses the trie: instead of checking against one word's characters, the DFS walks the trie alongside the board, checking whether the trie has a child matching the current board character; if not, that path is abandoned immediately, since no word continues that way.

The core idea: build one shared trie from every word, then run a single DFS backtracking search per starting cell that checks progress against every word simultaneously via the trie.

Build a trie containing every word, marking trie nodes that complete a word. From every board cell, run a DFS that walks the trie in lockstep with the board: if the trie has no child for the current cell's character, stop immediately; if the current trie node marks a complete word, record it; otherwise, continue to unvisited adjacent cells, marking the current cell used and restoring it afterward.
9. Optimized Solution

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: one DFS per cell, walking a shared trie instead of searching per word

blocks.text: Why This Works

Because every word's prefix is merged into a single trie, a DFS starting from a board cell checks its progress against every word sharing that prefix simultaneously, instead of repeating the same board walk once per word. The moment the trie has no child for the current character, the search knows immediately that no word (not just one) continues that way, pruning the entire subtree of possibilities at once.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(rows times cols times 4 to the power maximum word length), one shared DFS search overall, rather than one per word.
Space: O(total characters across all words) for the trie.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Word Search II is a direct combination of two techniques: DFS backtracking on a grid (from Word Search I), and merging many words into a shared trie so their common prefixes are searched only once, pruning entire groups of words the moment their shared prefix fails to continue.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting to un-mark a visited cell after backtracking, which would corrupt later searches from other starting cells.
Not removing a word from the trie (or otherwise marking it found) after it is discovered, which can cause duplicate results if the same word appears via multiple paths.
Building a separate trie search per word instead of one merged trie for all of them.

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Explicitly stating why merging words into a trie helps, "words sharing a prefix are explored together, and pruning happens for all of them at once", shows the key optimization insight clearly.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "searching per word seems slow with many words", think: merge every word into one trie, so shared prefixes are explored, and pruned, only once.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you remove a word from the trie once it has been found, to avoid rediscovering it via a different path?
How does this problem's complexity change with the board size versus the number and length of words?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Word Search I, the single-word version this problem extends.
Any "search for many strings against the same data" problem where merging them into a trie avoids repeated prefix work.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs independent searches per word; the optimized shared-trie DFS runs a single pass over the board, checking all words at once.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: DFS backtracking on a grid, guided by a trie merging every target word.
Core Idea: merge all words into one trie so a single DFS pass checks progress against every word simultaneously, pruning the instant no word continues the current path.
Time: O(words.length times rows times cols times 4^L) for the brute force, O(rows times cols times 4^L) for the optimized shared-trie approach.
Space: O(L) per search for the brute force, O(total word characters) for the trie in the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: words sharing a prefix can be searched together, and pruned together, using a single merged trie instead of independent searches.
Interview Difficulty: combines two well-known techniques, grid backtracking and tries, into a single, higher-value solution.
One line memory trick: merge every word into one trie; DFS the board once, walking the trie alongside it.
